title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
gist: AI data center developers, unwilling to wait up to a decade for grid connections, have announced 100+ US behind-the-meter gas plants (115+ GW, per Cleanview), though only ~4.9 GW operate and 15.8 GW are under construction. Turbine shortages push them toward less-efficient single-cycle units, raising emissions (BloombergNEF: +152 Mt CO2e/yr vs grid by 2035), lock-in risk, and household gas prices.

insights.claim: As of October 2026, US data center developers had announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter natural gas power plants with combined planned capacity above 115 GW, more than double California's peak power demand, per Cleanview data.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Signals a large potential demand pool for gas turbines, gas supply and midstream tied to AI data centers.

insights.claim: Only a small fraction of announced data-center gas capacity is real so far: 4.9 GW of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating and 15.8 GW are under construction, versus 115+ GW announced, per Cleanview.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Large announced-to-built gap means headline pipeline numbers overstate near-term gas/turbine demand; track conversion rate.

insights.so_what: Time-to-power is the binding constraint for AI capacity; assets that shorten it command premium pricing.

insights.claim: Gas turbine equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with surging demand from both utilities and data centers, pushing behind-the-meter developers toward less-efficient, cheaper single-cycle turbines rather than combined-cycle units.
